docker-host/deploy-from-github:
`miosa deploy create --git` clones a repository, builds the branch you name, and publishes it at a stable URL.
The same deployment rebuilds when you push, once you add its webhook to the repository.

## Connect GitHub

A public repository needs no connection.
A private repository is cloned with the GitHub connection of the person who creates the deployment, so connect GitHub first:

```bash
miosa connections add apps github
```

The command opens GitHub's consent page and waits until you approve.
In the console the same connection is under **Connections**, **Apps**.

GitHub shows MIOSA only the organizations that approved it.
If an organization's repositories are missing, grant access on GitHub under **Settings**, **Applications**, **Authorized OAuth Apps**, or ask an organization owner to approve MIOSA.

## Deploy a repository

```bash
miosa deploy create --git https://github.com/octocat/Spoon-Knife --branch main
```

The command waits until the deployment is live and prints its URL, for example `https://spoon-knife.<your-org>.miosa.app`.
Pass `--name` to choose the deployment name; it defaults to the repository name.
Pass `--no-wait` to return as soon as the deployment is created.

Name the branch with `--branch`.
The deployment builds that branch now and on every push to it.

A private repository works the same way once GitHub is connected.
Without the connection, or with a branch that does not exist, the build fails at the clone step:

```text
publishing failed at build: The source could not be cloned (git exited 128). (SOURCE_CLONE_FAILED)
```

Connect GitHub, check the branch name, and run `miosa deploy redeploy <name>`.

## Logs and builds

```bash
miosa deploy builds my-app     # every build and its state
miosa deploy logs my-app       # why the last build failed, and the app's output
```

A static site has no runtime log: it serves the built files and runs no process.

## Redeploy

```bash
miosa deploy redeploy my-app
```

Redeploy builds the branch again from GitHub and releases it.
Use it after you fix a failed build, or to pick up a change without a push.

## Rebuild on every push

When `deploy create --git` creates the deployment, it prints a webhook secret once:

```text
Add this GitHub webhook so pushes redeploy (the secret is shown once):
  URL:          https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/integrations/github/webhook
  Content type: application/json
  Secret:       <webhook secret>
  Events:       Just the push event
```

Add it to the repository under **Settings**, **Webhooks**, **Add webhook**, with exactly those values.
GitHub signs every delivery with the secret.
MIOSA checks the signature, finds the deployment for that repository and branch, and builds the pushed commit.
A delivery with no signature is refused with 401, and one with a wrong signature with 403.
Pushes to other branches are ignored.

The secret is also the `webhook_secret` field of the create response (`--json`).
Store it like a password: anyone with it can trigger a build.
To replace it, call `POST /api/v1/deployments/{id}/webhook-secret` and update the webhook on GitHub with the new value.

## Related

- [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing) explains how a build becomes a version.
- [Domains](/docs/docker-host/domains) attaches your own domain to the deployment.
- [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback) makes an earlier version live again.
docker-host/deployment-model:
Every publish turns a Sandbox into a stable production app backed by immutable versions, health checks, and a public URL returned by the API. This page explains the objects behind that flow and how they fit together. ## The deployment pipeline Every publish travels the same path: ```mermaid graph LR A[Sandbox] -->|publish| B[Source Snapshot] B --> C[Build] C -->|builds| D[Release] D -->|creates| E[Deployment Version] E -->|promotes| F[Static artifact, dynamic runtime or Docker Host container] F --> G[Domain] ``` 1. **Sandbox** - the mutable environment where you (or an agent) write code. 2. **Source Snapshot** - an immutable tarball of `/workspace` captured at publish time. The sandbox can keep changing; the snapshot is frozen. 3. **Build** - MIOSA runs the configured build/packaging pipeline from the frozen source. 4. **Release** - the immutable build output. Static: files/assets. Dynamic: a server app artifact with command, port, and health check. 5. **Deployment Version** - the row in history. `version_number` increases monotonically. Every version is bootable forever. 6. **Runtime** - for dynamic deployments, MIOSA starts a production runtime and health-checks it. Static releases skip this; MIOSA serves the files directly. Docker Host releases run as containers on the workspace Docker Host. 7. **Domain** - the route. Managed, workspace-owned, tenant-owned, or exact custom domain. Rollback is re-pointing this route with no rebuild. ## Static vs Dynamic | | Static | Dynamic | Docker Host | |---|---|---|---| | Source shape | HTML / JS / CSS / assets only | Server-side code | Many small workspace apps, funnels, APIs, client sites | | Build output | Files/assets | Server app artifact | Container image from a release artifact | | Production runtime | Static artifact serving, no per-app process | MIOSA dynamic runtime pool | Workspace Docker Host | | Scaling | Instant file serving | Scheduler manages desired instance count | Multiple app containers on one workspace host | | Rollback speed | Seconds | Seconds | Seconds after the replacement container is healthy | | Best for | Landing pages, SPAs, generated HTML, docs | APIs, SSR, WebSockets, background workers | Multi-app workspaces and white-label app factories | Pass `kind: "auto"` (or the SDK equivalent) and MIOSA chooses the static or dynamic path from your publish inputs. Supplying a run command and port makes the deployment dynamic. Use Docker Host when you explicitly want the app to run inside the workspace Docker Host. The recommended CLI path is: ```bash miosa deploy create --from-sandbox \ --name \ --type docker_deploy \ --wait \ --json ``` Use the same `--name` on every publish so MIOSA creates a new version behind the same deployment ID and URL. ## The deployment object A **Deployment** is the stable product object. It is the thing the world thinks of as "the live app." It has a name, a slug, an active version, and one or more domains pointing at it. ```mermaid flowchart LR P[Project] --> D["Deployment
team-portal"] D --> V17["active_version_id: Version 17
Release sha:abc..."] D --> V16["Version 16
archived, still bootable"] D --> V15["Version 15
archived, still bootable"] D --> DM[domains] DM --> D1["team-portal.example-org.miosa.app
managed fallback"] DM --> D2["team-portal.apps.example.com
tenant deployment domain"] DM --> D3["example.net
custom, verified"] D --> DA[data] DA --> PGS["postgres
DATABASE_URL=..."] ``` A Deployment URL is **stable**. New publishes change which version it points at, not the URL itself. ## What gets versioned | Thing | Versioned? | |---|---| | Source snapshot | Yes - sha256 of the tarball captured at publish time | | Release artifact | Yes - sha256 of the static files or dynamic server artifact | | Deployment Version | Yes - `version_number` monotonically increases | | Domain ↔ version mapping | Yes - change history retained | | Runtime Instances | Managed by scheduler against desired count; not versioned | | Data Services | Not versioned - Postgres / Redis / buckets persist across deploys | Rollback works because every release is immutable and stays in storage. Re-point the deployment at version 14 and MIOSA serves that known-good version again. The active version remains live while a candidate builds and starts. MIOSA changes production traffic only after the candidate passes its required checks. If the candidate fails, the active version remains unchanged. > **Note: Deployment products** > > Use `kind: "static"`, `kind: "dynamic"`, or `kind: "auto"` for standard MIOSA Deploy. > Use Docker Host when the deployment should become a container on the workspace Docker Host. > The internal API value is still `docker_deploy` for compatibility. ## Proof contract The deployment object is not the same thing as proof that production traffic is working. For standard deployments, proof means the deployment has a public URL and MIOSA can route to the active release. For Docker Host deployments, proof also requires the workspace host, durable app target, running container route, and public URL probe. Use: ```bash miosa deploy get --json miosa deploy requests ``` ## See also - [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing): The sandbox-to-version pipeline: source snapshots, build modes, and promotion. - [Versions](/docs/docker-host/versions): Immutable history. List, inspect, promote, and archive versions. - [Docker Hosts](/docs/docker-host/hosts): The workspace host that runs Docker Host containers.
docker-host/docker-deploy:
Docker Host is MIOSA's dedicated workspace host model for customers that need many small apps, funnels, lead magnets, APIs, or client sites without creating a new production VM for every deployment.
It is the recommended production path for generated apps that should run 24/7 inside a workspace.
MIOSA keeps routing, domains, and attribution as the source of truth, and the host supplies the execution capacity.

## 1. Ensure the workspace host

```bash
miosa api POST /docker-deploy/hosts/ensure -d '{"workspace_id": "<workspace-id>"}'
miosa api GET /docker-deploy/hosts?workspace_id=<workspace-id>
```

The host moves from `provisioning` to `bootstrapping` to `active`. Publishes wait until it is active.

## 2. Publish an app

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --name my-app \
  --dir /workspace \
  --run-command "npm run start" \
  --port 3000 \
  --type docker_deploy \
  --wait \
  --wait-timeout 900s \
  --json
```

To publish a new version without changing the deployment URL, reuse the same `--name`.

## 3. Prove it

```bash
miosa deploy get <deployment-id> --json
```

A Docker Host deployment is live only when the host is active, the app target is running, the container route is reachable, and a probe to `public_url` succeeds.

docker-host/domains:
A **Domain** is a hostname that routes to a preview, a deployment, a computer, or an exact custom resource. For production deployments, always use the `public_url` returned by the API. Do not reconstruct hostnames in SDKs, CLIs, or frontends.

## Domain layers

MIOSA keeps these layers separate:

| Layer | URL shape | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Sandbox preview domain | `https://{port}-{sandbox_slug}.sandbox.{preview_domain}` | Mutable live previews while an agent/user is editing |
| Tenant deployment domain | `https://{deployment_slug}.{deployment_domain}` | Branded durable URLs for generated production apps |
| Managed fallback domain | `https://{deployment_slug}.{organization_slug}.miosa.app` | Always-available MIOSA-managed fallback |
| Exact custom domain | `https://customer-owned.example.com` | A customer's chosen production domain attached to one deployment |
| Computer custom domain | `https://desktop.customer-owned.example.com` | A customer-owned hostname attached to one computer service |

Lumen is a made-up company, and `example.com` and `example.net` are reserved example domains.
Replace them with your own.

Lumen example:

```text
Sandbox preview:   https://5173-abc123.sandbox.example.com
Deployment domain: https://lead-magnet.apps.example.com
Managed fallback:  https://lead-magnet.example-org.miosa.app
Custom domain:     https://portal.example.net
```

Preview domains do not imply production deployment domains. Configure both if you want both surfaces branded.

## Tenant deployment domains

Tenant deployment domains are configured separately from preview domains. The backend resolves `settings["deployment_domain"]` for durable app URLs and falls back to `{organization_slug}.miosa.app` when no deployment domain is configured.

Public tenant-level management routes for deployment domains are not exposed yet. Operators can configure the tenant setting; SDKs and CLIs should treat deployment `public_url` / `url` as authoritative.

Recommended white-label DNS:

| Record type | Name | Value | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CNAME` | `*` | `proxy.miosa.ai` | Preview domain, including sandbox port previews |
| `CNAME` | `*.apps` | `proxy.miosa.ai` | Durable generated apps |

## Exact custom domains

Exact custom domains attach a customer-owned hostname to one deployment.
Exact custom domains are enabled by plan: Developer includes 3, Business 100 and Enterprise 500, with no support ticket. A Developer plan that has used all three gets `PLAN_LIMIT_REACHED` from the same check as any other cap.

| Kind | Example | DNS record |
|---|---|---|
| Subdomain | `app.example.net` | `CNAME` to the verification target |
| Apex | `example.net` | `A`/`AAAA`, `ALIAS`, `ANAME`, or flattened `CNAME` depending on DNS provider |
| WWW alias | `www.example.net` | `CNAME` to the verification target |

## The attach flow

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// 1. Register the exact domain. MIOSA returns DNS instructions.
const domain = await miosa.deployments.domains.add(deploymentId, {
  domain: "portal.example.net",
})

console.log(domain.dns_records)

// 2. After records are set, ask MIOSA to verify.
await miosa.deployments.domains.verify(deploymentId, domain.id)

// 3. Use the deployment public_url returned by the API.
const deployment = await miosa.deployments.get(deploymentId)
console.log(deployment.public_url)
```

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key="msk_u_...")

domain = miosa.deployments.domains(deployment_id).add(
    domain="portal.example.net",
)

for record in domain.get("dns_records", []):
    print(record["type"], record["name"], record["value"])

miosa.deployments.domains(deployment_id).verify(domain["id"])

deployment = miosa.deployments.get(deployment_id)
print(deployment["public_url"])
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/domains \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"domain":"portal.example.net"}'

curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/domains/$DOMAIN_ID/verify \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

Once verified and TLS-active, MIOSA routes the exact domain to the deployment's active version. Exact custom domains take precedence over tenant deployment domains and MIOSA fallback URLs.

## Redirect policy

For apex + www domains, set the redirect policy:

| Policy | Result |
|---|---|
| `none` | Both apex and www serve independently |
| `apex_to_www` | `example.net` redirects to `www.example.net` |
| `www_to_apex` | `www.example.net` redirects to `example.net` |

Configure at attach time or update later via `PATCH /deployments/:id/domains/:domain_id`.

## What changing a domain does

Changing a domain mapping:

- Updates MIOSA's route table.
- Takes effect within seconds.
- Does **not** rebuild the app.
- Does **not** involve the source sandbox.
- Does **not** require users to change the deployment ID.

This is why rollback is fast: only the deployment's active version/route changes.

## DNS verification edge cases

| Situation | Behavior |
|---|---|
| CNAME points to the wrong host | Verification fails with `dns_target_mismatch`. Show the expected target. |
| TXT record not propagated yet | Verification fails with `dns_propagation_pending`. Retry after a few minutes. |
| User typos the domain | Verification fails with `dns_resolution_error`. Domain stays pending. |
| Domain already attached to another deployment in your tenant | `409 Conflict`. Detach from the other deployment first. |
| Domain attached to a different tenant | `403 Forbidden`. Contact support for transfer. |

## Provider input fields

DNS providers label the same fields differently.

Use the exact values MIOSA returns and translate only the field name:

| MIOSA instruction | Common provider labels | Example for `*.apps.example.com` |
|---|---|---|
| Record type | Type | `CNAME` |
| Host | Name, Host, Alias | `*.apps` |
| Target | Value, Points to, Destination | `proxy.miosa.ai` |
| TTL | TTL, Cache time | Automatic or 300 seconds |

Do not enter `https://`, a path, or a trailing slash in a DNS target.

Disable provider proxying until MIOSA reports that ownership and TLS verification are complete.

## Verification sequence

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Register hostname"] --> B["Copy exact DNS records"]
  B --> C["Authoritative DNS answers"]
  C --> D["MIOSA verifies ownership"]
  D --> E["Certificate becomes active"]
  E --> F["Route serves active Version"]
```

If DNS resolves but the page still fails, continue with the [Recovery Playbooks](/docs/operations/recovery) instead of changing records repeatedly.

## White-label checklist

For a platform like Lumen:

1. Configure the organization slug (`lumen`).
2. Configure preview DNS: a wildcard `CNAME` named `*` on `example.com`, pointing to `proxy.miosa.ai`.
3. Configure tenant deployment DNS, for example `*.apps.example.com`.
4. Publish generated apps and display the returned deployment `public_url`.
5. Attach exact customer domains only when a customer brings its own domain.

> **Note: Current V1 rule**
>
> Preview domains, deployment domains, computer URLs, and exact custom domains are separate. Use the URL returned by the backend for each resource: `preview_url`, `desktop_url`, or deployment `public_url`.

## Set up a custom domain in the dashboard

Connect your own domain - for example `app.example.com` - so users land on your brand rather than a MIOSA fallback URL.

Go to **Settings → Domains** and click **+ Add custom domain**. The wizard walks you through three steps:

1. Enter your domain (`app.example.com`  -  no `https://`, no trailing path).
2. Add the DNS records shown to your domain provider.
3. Click **Continue to verify**  -  MIOSA checks your DNS and activates the domain.

You can also register the domain through the exact deployment or computer domain APIs before sending traffic; MIOSA returns the DNS records and verification status.

### Required DNS records

For wildcard preview or app domains, delegate traffic to MIOSA:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Type | `CNAME` |
| Host | `*` (wildcard) |
| Value | `proxy.miosa.ai` |
| TTL | `300` - `600` seconds |
| Proxy status (Cloudflare only) | **DNS only**  -  gray cloud |

Replace `yourdomain.com` with the apex domain you own (e.g. `example.com` if your custom domain is `app.example.com`).

> **Apex domains** (no subdomain, e.g. `example.com` directly) additionally require an A/ALIAS record  -  add `_miosa-verify.example.com TXT <token>` as shown in the wizard.

> **Caution: Important if you use Cloudflare DNS**
>
> If you're using Cloudflare as your DNS provider, make sure the wildcard CNAME has the proxy status set to **DNS only** (gray cloud), not **Proxied** (orange cloud). When proxied, Cloudflare terminates TLS itself and MIOSA never receives the request to issue a certificate  -  your sandbox URLs will fail with a TLS error. Other DNS providers (Route 53, Namecheap, GoDaddy, Porkbun) don't have this issue.

### TLS certificates and propagation

Certificates are provisioned automatically once DNS propagates. There is nothing to upload. You will see a valid `https://` certificate on first browser visit.

DNS changes typically take **5-30 minutes** but can take up to 48 hours depending on your provider's TTL settings.

To check current propagation status:

```bash
dig *.yourdomain.com CNAME +short
```

The expected result is `proxy.miosa.ai.`

Once configured and verified, MIOSA's router confirms the hostname belongs to your tenant, workspace, project, computer, or deployment, issues or reuses the TLS certificate, and routes the request to the current sandbox, computer, standard deployment, or Docker Host container. Domain ownership and tenant scope are checked before MIOSA routes traffic.

## Troubleshooting a routed domain

**Verification fails immediately after adding records**  -  DNS propagation is not instant. Wait a few minutes and click **Retry verification** in the wizard. The wizard polls every 5 seconds while open.

**`dig` shows the right value but verification still fails**  -  Some DNS providers add extra trailing dots or spaces. Ensure the CNAME value is exactly `proxy.miosa.ai` with no extra characters.

**Cache flush**  -  If the record still shows the old value, flush your local DNS cache:

```bash
# macOS
sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder

# Linux (systemd-resolved)
sudo systemd-resolve --flush-caches
```

Or check propagation from a neutral vantage point using [dnschecker.org](https://dnschecker.org/).

**My sandbox URL returns a TLS error or cert warning**  -  DNS hasn't propagated yet, or (on Cloudflare) the proxy status is not **DNS only**. Confirm the record with `dig +short "*.your-domain.com" CNAME` (expected `proxy.miosa.ai.`).

**My sandbox URL returns 502 or 503**  -  Your sandbox isn't running, or no HTTP server is listening on the port you're requesting. The DNS chain is correct; the sandbox just needs to serve traffic.

**My sandbox URL returns 400 or "URL not connected"**  -  The slug doesn't match any sandbox in your tenant. Confirm the sandbox is in `running` state and that the slug (first 8 hex chars of the sandbox UUID) matches the leftmost label of the hostname.

## Branding

Once your domain is connected, customize the app name, logo, accent color, and favicon at **Settings → General → Branding**. The Domains page shows a live preview of what your users will see.

## Disconnecting

To stop using your custom domain: remove the CNAME from your DNS provider, or open **Settings → Domains** in MIOSA and click **Disconnect**. After disconnecting, the next request to `<slug>.<your-domain>` will fail to issue a certificate. The domain becomes available to bind to a different tenant after the cache expires.

docker-host/environments:
A **Deployment Environment** is the scope at which env vars, secrets, and data service bindings apply. Most projects have at least two: `production` and `staging`. Custom environments like `preview/feature-abc` are common for review-app workflows.

> **Note: Phase status**
>
> First-class `deployment_environments` records are part of the ongoing deployment refactor. Today, env vars are scoped per-deployment via `deployment_env_vars`. The shape and behavior here are the steady-state target.

## Defaults

Every project gets two environments at creation:

- `production`: what real users see
- `staging`: internal testing target before promoting to production

You can create additional environments (`preview/<source>`, `qa`, `canary`, etc.) as needed.

## What environments scope

| Item | Scope |
|---|---|
| Env vars | per environment |
| Secrets | per environment |
| Data service bindings (DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, etc.) | per environment |
| Domains | per environment (production gets the apex; staging gets a `staging.*` subdomain by convention) |
| Version promotion | per environment, promote a version to staging first, then to production |

The same deployment can run different versions in different environments. Common pattern:
```text

production:   version 17 active
staging:      version 18 active   ← being tested
preview/pr-42: version 19 active  ← single-feature preview
```

## Env vars
```http
POST /api/v1/deployments/:id/env
GET  /api/v1/deployments/:id/env
```

Env vars are stored encrypted at rest (ChaCha20-Poly1305) and injected into the sandbox during development and into runtime instances at boot. The list endpoint returns previews of values, not the raw values, by default.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await miosa.deployments.env.set(deploymentId, {
  environment: "production",
  vars: {
    STRIPE_KEY: "sk_live_...",
    NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: "https://api.example.net",
  },
})

const preview = await miosa.deployments.env.list(deploymentId, {
  environment: "production",
})
// preview returns: { STRIPE_KEY: "sk_live_••••", NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: "https://api…" }
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/env \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "environment": "production",
    "vars": { "STRIPE_KEY": "sk_live_..." }
  }'
```

## Secrets vs env vars

There's no strict UI distinction today: env vars are encrypted at rest regardless. The convention is:

- **Env vars**: configuration that can be retrieved as preview (truncated value).
- **Secrets**: same encryption, but marked `is_secret: true` so previews always show `••••` even to your own admins.

Future-state, secrets will support rotation and access-event audit logging.

## Data service bindings

When you create a Postgres / Redis / bucket via [Data](/docs/data/overview), you bind it to a specific deployment environment. MIOSA injects the credential into env at boot:
```text

production env:    DATABASE_URL=postgres://prod...
staging env:       DATABASE_URL=postgres://staging...
```

You don't ship two database URLs for one app; you ship one connection string variable, and MIOSA picks the right value based on which environment the runtime is booted in.

- [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing): environments are picked at publish time
- [Domains](/docs/docker-host/domains): attach a staging subdomain
- [Data](/docs/data/overview): environment-scoped credentials
docker-host/hosts:
A Docker Host host is the always-on workspace VM that runs Docker Host containers.
This page covers the host model, its lifecycle, how a publish reaches it, and how MIOSA proves the app is live.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SB[Sandbox] --> REL[MIOSA release artifact]
    REL --> IMG[Docker image]
    IMG --> HOST[Workspace Docker Host]
    HOST --> APP1[Local app container]
    HOST --> APP2[Local app container]
    HOST --> APP3[Local app container]
    APP1 --> ROUTER[MIOSA router and domains]
```

When Docker Host is enabled for a workspace, MIOSA provisions one always-on Docker Host VM for that workspace. That host runs:

1. A white-labeled Docker Host portal for the workspace.
2. The private Docker Host control service.
3. One or more app containers created from immutable release artifacts.

The deployment still belongs to the MIOSA organization, workspace, project, and deployment records. The Docker host is execution capacity, not an authorization boundary.

Docker Host is not a label on a normal dynamic runtime.
For Docker Host publishes, MIOSA must wait for the workspace host and private agent to be ready before the deployment can be marked ready.
If the host is not active, the publish response stays pending instead of falling back to the standard runtime pool.

Docker Host apps are launched as isolated containers on the workspace host.
MIOSA records each app target durably so routing and recovery do not depend on transient process state.

## Host lifecycle

Create or inspect the workspace host before publishing customer apps:

```bash
miosa api POST /docker-deploy/hosts/ensure -d '{"workspace_id": "<workspace-id>"}'
miosa api GET /docker-deploy/hosts?workspace_id=<workspace-id>
```

The host moves through provisioning states until the Docker Host runtime is reachable and passes health checks.

| State           | Meaning                                                                                 |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `provisioning`  | MIOSA is creating or starting the workspace Computer.                                   |
| `bootstrapping` | The portal and private deployment agent are being installed.                            |
| `active`        | The host is healthy and can accept Docker Host publishes.                                |
| `failed`        | MIOSA could not provision or bootstrap the host. Retry after fixing the reported issue. |

Each enabled workspace normally has one Docker Host. That host can run many app containers, and MIOSA still accounts deployments individually by organization, workspace, project, and deployment.

## Default URL behavior

Until a custom domain is attached, MIOSA returns a managed URL.
For a deployment in the OSA tenant, that can look like:

```text
https://my-app.osa.miosa.app
```

If the organization configures its own preview or deployment domain, workspace and project deployments can use that domain instead:

```text
intake.example.com
program.example.net
```

The exact URL is always returned by the publish/deploy response. Do not construct it in your app.
The effective URL hierarchy is:

1. Deployment custom domain.
2. Workspace deployment domain.
3. Tenant deployment domain.
4. MIOSA-managed tenant URL at `https://<deployment-slug>.<tenant-slug>.miosa.app`.

## Workspace and project scoping

Docker Host follows the same MIOSA attribution model as sandboxes and normal deployments:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Org[Organization] --> Workspace[Workspace]
  Workspace --> Project[Project]
  Project --> Sandbox[Sandbox]
  Project --> Deployment[Deployment]
  Project --> Domains[Domains]
  Project --> Data[Data services]
```

For multi-tenant products, pass your external IDs when creating workspaces, projects, sandboxes, and deployments. MIOSA stores those for billing, support, and customer mapping.

> **Note: Lumen example**
>
> Lumen can create one workspace per customer or expert. Each workspace can have many projects and many sandbox-created deployments. Those deployments can stay on Lumen's managed domain or move to a customer-owned domain like `program.example.net`.

## Publishing to Docker Host

Use Docker Host when you want a sandbox artifact to run on the workspace Docker host instead of the standard dynamic runtime pool.

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --name my-app \
  --dir /workspace \
  --run-command "npm run start" \
  --port 3000 \
  --type docker_deploy \
  --wait \
  --wait-timeout 900s \
  --json
```

To publish a new version without changing the deployment URL, reuse the same `--name`.

The platform flow is:

1. Freeze the sandbox files into a release artifact.
2. Ensure the workspace Docker Host is active.
3. Upload the release to that workspace host.
4. Build the release into a Docker image.
5. Run the image as a local Docker container on the host.
6. Record the durable app target and runtime route.
7. Register MIOSA routing to the returned host port.
8. Return the live deployment URL.

If the host is still provisioning, the API returns `ready: false` instead of silently serving the app through a standard runtime.

## Proving Docker Host deployments

A Docker Host deployment is live only when all of these are true:

| Proof item | Required state |
| ---------- | -------------- |
| Deployment row | Exists and has `deployment_product: "docker_deploy"` |
| Host link | `docker_deploy_host_id` points to the workspace Docker Host |
| Host health | Host is active and reachable |
| App target | The deployment has a durable running Docker Host target |
| Container route | The active target has a reachable container route |
| Public URL | HTTP probe to `public_url` succeeds |

Use:

```bash
miosa deploy get <deployment-id> --json
```

## Updates and recovery

Every publish creates a candidate release.
MIOSA keeps the current healthy version serving until the candidate is built, started, health checked, routed, and promoted.
A failed candidate does not replace the live version.

Host maintenance can briefly interrupt apps on that host.
MIOSA preserves deployment records, release artifacts, domains, data bindings, and desired state while the host is updated.
Deployments that were running are reconciled and verified before the host returns to active service.

An intentionally stopped deployment remains stopped.
MIOSA does not treat a deliberate stop as a recovery target.

After maintenance, check the deployment's public contract and, for Docker Host, the host it runs on:

```bash
miosa deploy get <deployment-id> --json
miosa api GET /docker-deploy/hosts/<host-id>
```

## Runtime boundary

Docker Host uses two different host-side services:

| Service | Visibility                 | Purpose                                           |
| ------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Portal  | User-facing, white-labeled | Shows the workspace deployment center.            |
| Agent   | MIOSA-private network only | Receives release artifacts and starts containers. |

Never expose the agent URL, Docker socket, host IP, or internal API key to browsers or customer code. SDKs, MCP tools, and customer apps should call MIOSA APIs; MIOSA talks to the workspace host.

## Domains

Domains can be set at several levels:

| Level        | Example                     | Use                                        |
| ------------ | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Organization | `example.com`              | Default customer preview/deployment domain |
| Workspace    | `acme.example.com`      | Client or expert workspace domain          |
| Deployment   | `program.example.net` | Exact app/site/funnel domain               |

MIOSA still verifies DNS, issues TLS, and routes traffic. The Docker Host only runs the app containers.

## What users see

Customers see MIOSA or your white-labeled product language. They should not see provider names, raw host IPs, Docker socket details, or internal agent URLs.

## API and SDKs

Use the Docker Host APIs when your app needs to prepare a workspace before a publish:

```text
GET  /api/v1/docker-deploy/hosts?workspace_id=<workspace-id>
POST /api/v1/docker-deploy/hosts/ensure
GET  /api/v1/docker-deploy/hosts/:id
```

The TypeScript and Python SDKs expose the same host operations. MCP tools are available for agents that need to check or ensure the workspace host before publishing.

For running a project's web services, workers, schedules and static sites, use [Services](/docs/services/overview) instead.

The pages below describe the Docker Host deployment model.

Deploying on MIOSA means turning a Sandbox into a stable production app, site, or API backed by immutable versions, health checks, and a public URL returned by the API.
Once published, the deployment URL stays stable.
New publishes change which version it points at.

## 1. Publish from a sandbox

**CLI**

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --name <deployment> \
  --type docker_deploy \
  --wait \
  --json
```

Use the same `--name` on every publish so MIOSA creates a new version behind the same deployment ID and URL.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const result = await miosa.deployments.publish(deploymentId, {
  sourceSandboxId: sandbox.id,
  kind: "auto",                       // "static" | "dynamic" | "auto"
  environment: "production",          // "production" | "staging" | etc.
  outputPath: "/workspace",
  runCommand: "npm start",            // dynamic deployments only
  port: 3000,                         // dynamic only
})

console.log(result.deployment.public_url)
console.log(result.version.kind, result.version.state)
```

**Python**

```python
result = miosa.deployments.publish(
    deployment_id,
    source_sandbox_id=sandbox_id,
    kind="auto",              # "static" | "dynamic" | "auto"
    environment="production",
    output_path="/workspace",
    run_command="npm start",         # dynamic only
    port=3000,                       # dynamic only
)

print(result.deployment.public_url)
print(result.version.kind, result.version.state)
```

## 2. Promote or roll back

```bash
miosa deploy releases <deployment>
miosa deploy promote <deployment> <release>
miosa deploy rollback <deployment> --to <release-id> --yes --json
```

Promotion and rollback each target one exact immutable release.

## 3. Prove it is live

```bash
miosa deploy get <deployment> --json
miosa deploy requests <deployment>
```

A deployment object is not proof by itself.
The public URL must route to the active release, and for Docker Host also to the workspace host and a running container.

docker-host/publishing:
Publish is the moment a mutable sandbox becomes a frozen, reproducible artifact ready to serve production traffic.
The final runtime can be standard MIOSA Deploy or Docker Host.
The public URL always comes from MIOSA.

## The pipeline
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SB[Sandbox] -->|freeze /workspace| SS[Source Snapshot]
    SS --> BLD[Build]
    BLD -->|compile + package| REL[Release]
    REL -->|referenced by| VER[Deployment Version]
    VER -->|promote| DEP[Deployment]
    DEP -->|standard deploy or Docker Host| DOM[Domain]
```

1. Sandbox /workspace          (mutable; agent or developer is editing here)
2. Source snapshot             (tarball, sha256-keyed, stored in object storage)
3. Build                       (static packager, auto-detect, or explicit commands)
4. Release                     (static artifact or dynamic server artifact, sha256-keyed)
5. Deployment Version          (database row pointing at the release)
6. Health check                (for dynamic; static skips this)
7. Promotion                   (Deployment.active_version_id updated)
8. Proof                       (route, runtime, and URL verified)

The sequence below shows who acts at each step:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant YC as Your Code
    participant M as MIOSA

    YC->>M: publish sandbox to new or existing deployment
    M-->>YC: 202 Accepted (build in progress)
    M->>M: freeze /workspace → source snapshot
    M->>M: compile + package → release artifact
    M->>M: create Deployment Version row
    M->>M: health check (dynamic only)
    M->>M: promote  -  Deployment.active_version_id updated
    M-->>YC: version.state = ready, public_url live
```

You make one publish request.
MIOSA does all of this internally and returns the result when the version reaches a terminal state.
For Docker Host, MIOSA also ensures the workspace host, starts the app container, and proves the route before the deployment is treated as live.

## The publish call

**CLI**

Create the deployment from a tested sandbox:

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --name my-app \
  --dir /workspace \
  --type docker_deploy \
  --wait \
  --json
```

Publish the next version to that same deployment:

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --name <deployment> \
  --dir /workspace \
  --type docker_deploy \
  --wait \
  --json
```

The second command preserves the deployment ID and canonical URL.
It creates a new immutable candidate and promotes it only after verification succeeds.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const result = await miosa.deployments.publish(deploymentId, {
  sourceSandboxId: sandbox.id,
  kind: "auto",                       // "static" | "dynamic" | "auto"
  environment: "production",          // "production" | "staging" | etc.
  outputPath: "/workspace",
  buildCommand: "npm run build",      // optional; auto-detected if omitted
  runCommand: "npm start",            // dynamic deployments only
  port: 3000,                         // dynamic only
  healthCheckPath: "/_health",        // dynamic only
  externalWorkspaceId: "acct-123",
  externalUserId: "user-456",
  externalProjectId: "landing-page-789",
})

console.log(result.deployment.public_url)
console.log(result.version.kind, result.version.state)
```

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key="msk_u_...")

result = miosa.deployments.publish(
    deployment_id,
    source_sandbox_id=sandbox_id,
    kind="auto",              # "static" | "dynamic" | "auto"
    environment="production",
    output_path="/workspace",
    build_command="npm run build",   # optional; auto-detected if omitted
    run_command="npm start",         # dynamic only
    port=3000,                       # dynamic only
    health_check_path="/_health",    # dynamic only
    external_workspace_id="acct-123",
    external_user_id="user-456",
    external_project_id="landing-page-789",

print(result.deployment.public_url)
print(result.version.kind, result.version.state)
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/publish \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \
  -d '{
    "source_sandbox_id": "'$SBX'",
    "kind": "auto",
    "environment": "production",
    "output_path": "/workspace",
    "build_command": "npm run build",
    "run_command": "npm start",
    "port": 3000,
    "health_check_path": "/_health"
  }'
```

Response shape:
```json
{
  "data": {
    "deployment": {
      "id": "dep_...",
      "active_version_id": "ver_...",
      "state": "running",
      "public_url": "https://team-portal.apps.example.com"
    },
    "version": {
      "id": "ver_...",
      "kind": "static",
      "state": "ready",
      "artifact_sha256": "...",
      "source_sha256": "..."
    },
    "services": [
      { "id": "svc_...", "type": "static_web", "state": "healthy" }
    ],
    "promoted": true
  }
}
```

## Source snapshots

Before the builder runs, MIOSA freezes a snapshot of the sandbox's source. The snapshot is a tarball of `/workspace` (or whatever `output_path` you specify), excluding cache directories that don't need to ship:
```text

included:    application code, package manifests, lockfiles, public assets, config
excluded:    node_modules, .next/cache, dist (will be rebuilt), .git (unless needed),
             __pycache__, build/, target/
```

The snapshot is stored and sha256-keyed. The version record stores `source_sha256` so retries can rebuild from the exact same input without re-snapshotting.

The sandbox keeps running while the build runs. You can keep editing.

## Build modes

MIOSA picks a build mode from the source. You can override with `build_command` if needed.

| Mode | Trigger | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Dockerfile** | `Dockerfile` exists in `output_path` | MIOSA builds the container-style server artifact |
| **Auto-detect** | `package.json` / `requirements.txt` / `pyproject.toml` / `go.mod` / `mix.exs` | MIOSA picks install/build/start defaults |
| **Static packager** | Only static files in output (no server entrypoint detected) | Files are stored as a static release |
| **Explicit** | `buildCommand` and/or `runCommand` provided | MIOSA runs those, then packages whatever's in `output_path` |

> **Caution: URL rule**
>
> Do not construct production URLs in your SDK, CLI, or frontend. Read `data.deployment.public_url` or `data.url` from the publish response and display that exact value. Tenants can use a deployment domain, MIOSA fallback, or an exact custom domain.

## Docker Host publish

Use Docker Host for workspaces that publish many small apps, funnels, lead magnets, APIs, or client sites.
The app runs as a container on the workspace Docker Host, while MIOSA owns routing, TLS, domains, billing attribution, and the Deployment record.

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --name my-app \
  --dir /workspace \
  --run-command "npm run start" \
  --port 3000 \
  --type docker_deploy \
  --wait \
  --wait-timeout 900s \
  --json
```

For an update, reuse the deployment `--name`.
This targets the existing deployment instead of creating another one.

Then check the deployment:

```bash
miosa deploy get <deployment-id> --json
miosa deploy requests <deployment-id>
```

The command name and API path still contain `docker-deploy` because that is the compatibility wire value.
Customer-facing product language is Docker Host.

## What gets promoted, and when

Static publishes promote as soon as the artifact is uploaded  -  there's nothing to health-check.

Dynamic publishes don't promote until:

1. The build succeeded.
2. The dynamic release artifact was stored.
3. New production runtimes were scheduled.
4. Health checks (`GET healthCheckPath`) returned 2xx for the configured grace period (default 30s healthy before promotion).

If health checks fail, the **previous version stays live** and the new version is marked `failed`. No traffic is sent to the broken release. Your last known good production keeps serving.

## Idempotency

Pass `Idempotency-Key` on every publish. If the same key is sent twice within the retention window, MIOSA returns the original result without re-building. This makes retries safe  -  useful for shaky network connections and worker queues.

## Failure modes

| Failure | What happens | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| Build command exits non-zero | Version marked `failed`, log uploaded, production unchanged | Fix in sandbox, publish again |
| Health check never passes | Version marked `failed`, runtime instances torn down | Fix run command or healthCheckPath, publish again |
| Docker Host is not active | Publish waits or returns not ready | Run `miosa api POST /docker-deploy/hosts/ensure`, then publish again |
| Docker Host app row is missing | The deployment is not routable | Re-publish with `--type docker_deploy --wait`, then check again |
| Source snapshot fails | Publish returns 5xx immediately, no version row created | Retry the request |
| Static build exceeds artifact size limit | Version marked `failed` | Reduce assets or contact support to raise limit |
| Two publishes race for the same deployment | Second one waits on the advisory lock; both eventually succeed in order | None  -  handled automatically by our operation lock |

docker-host/releases:
A **Release** is the immutable artifact produced by a build. Versions reference releases; static deployments serve files from them and dynamic deployments start runtimes from them.

You typically don't address releases directly through the API. They're an implementation detail of `Deployment Version`. But it's useful to know they exist as their own record because they're what makes rollback and horizontal scaling work.

> **Note: Caller contract**
>
> Most integrations do not need to read release records directly. Use deployment versions and the returned deployment `public_url` unless you are building an operator dashboard or audit workflow.

## Release kinds

| Kind | Used by | Storage |
|---|---|---|
| `static` | Static deployments | Built files and assets |
| `oci` | Dynamic deployments via OCI-compatible workflows | Server image artifact |
| `dynamic` | Server apps with a run command and port | Packaged server artifact |

The release format determines how the deployment is served:

- **Static releases** → MIOSA's static artifact server streams files from object storage directly. No per-app process runs.
- **Dynamic releases** → MIOSA starts healthy production runtimes and routes traffic to them.

## Immutability

Releases are content-addressed by sha256. A release with sha256 `abc...` is always the same bytes, anywhere it's referenced. This is what makes:

- **Rollback** trivial: repoint a domain at an older version, which still references its release.
- **Scaling** trivial: schedule N copies of the same release on N hosts; every instance is byte-identical.
- **Audit** clean: the release that served traffic at time T can be reproduced from its hash.

A release is never mutated after creation. To "change" it, publish a new version, which produces a new release.

## Where releases live

Releases are stored and served by MIOSA. You can inspect release metadata on the version record:
```json
{
  "version_number": 17,
  "artifact_sha256": "a5e6f0c1...",
  "artifact_manifest": {
    "files": 42,
    "total_bytes": 184320,
    "entrypoint": "index.html"
  }
}
```

You do not need to download releases yourself. The metadata is shown for debugging and audit.

## Source snapshot vs release

These are two different artifacts in the same build:

| Artifact | What it is | Sha256 stored on |
|---|---|---|
| **Source snapshot** | Frozen tarball of the sandbox source at publish time | `version.source_sha256` |
| **Release** | The built output | `version.artifact_sha256` |

The source snapshot exists so retries / rebuilds are reproducible. The release exists so production can be served and scaled.

## Garbage collection

Static release artifacts older than the retention window (default 30 days for archived versions) may be garbage-collected. The version row remains for audit; if you attempt to rollback to a version whose artifact has been GC'd, MIOSA returns 410 Gone.

Active versions (`active_version_id` on any deployment) are never GC'd, even past retention.

## See also

- [Versions](/docs/docker-host/versions): the record referencing the release
- [Dynamic Runtimes](/docs/docker-host/runtime-instances): what serves dynamic releases
- [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing): how releases are created
docker-host/rollback:
Rollback on MIOSA is fast because nothing has to be rebuilt. The previous release is still in storage. Runtime instances boot quickly. Static artifacts are streamed from object storage. The whole operation is "change one row, propagate to the edge cache."

## When you'd rollback

- New version passed health checks but the app is broken in real traffic (e.g. a feature flag mis-fire).
- A bad migration deployed.
- A regression you missed in staging.
- Hostile incident: quick revert while you investigate.

## How fast

| Step | Static | Dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| Update active version | `<1s` | `<1s` |
| Edge route cache refresh | `<60s default` | `<60s default` |
| New runtime instances spawn? | n/a (no per-app process) | Only if older version's instances were torn down; the scheduler boots replacements |
| Drain old runtime instances | n/a | Only if rolling forward, not on rollback |
| **Total wall clock** | **seconds** | **seconds to ~1 minute** |

If the older version's runtime instances are still healthy (recent rollforward where the old instances haven't been torn down yet), dynamic rollback is also instant: the router switches backends without any VM boots.

## How rollback works
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant API as Deployments API
    participant DB as active_version_id
    participant E as Edge routers
    participant RI as Runtime Instances

    C->>API: POST /deployments/:id/rollback { version_id }
    API->>DB: UPDATE active_version_id = version_id
    API->>E: invalidate route cache
    E-->>E: reload route table (<60s)
    API->>RI: confirm healthy instances for old version
    RI-->>API: instances ready
    API-->>C: deployment with new active_version_id
```

## API

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// Easy form: roll back to the previous version
await miosa.deployments.rollback(deploymentId)

// Explicit form: roll back to a specific version
await miosa.deployments.rollback(deploymentId, {
  versionId: "ver_01H...",
})
```

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key="msk_u_...")

# Easy form: roll back to the previous version
deployment = miosa.deployments.rollback(deployment_id)

# Explicit form: roll back to a specific version
deployment = miosa.deployments.rollback(
    deployment_id,
    version_id="ver_01H...",
)

print(deployment.active_version_id)
print(deployment.state)
```

**cURL**

```bash
# Rollback to a specific version
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/rollback \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \
  -d '{"version_id":"ver_01H..."}'
```

Server behavior:
```text

1. Validate target version_id belongs to this deployment
2. Validate target version state === "ready" (cannot rollback to failed)
3. Validate target version's release artifact still exists in storage
   (returns 410 Gone if GC'd)
4. UPDATE deployments SET active_version_id = $version_id
5. Invalidate edge route cache
6. For dynamic: confirm enough healthy instances for the old version; spawn if needed
7. Return the deployment with the new active_version_id
```

Response:
```json
{
  "data": {
    "id": "dep_...",
    "active_version_id": "ver_01H...",
    "state": "running",
    "public_url": "https://team-portal.example-org.miosa.app"
  }
}
```

## Picking the rollback target

Use the [Versions](/docs/docker-host/versions) API to inspect candidates:
```typescript
const versions = await miosa.deployments.versions.list(deploymentId, {
  state: "ready",
  limit: 10,
})

// Find the last known good version
const target = versions.data.find(v => v.id !== deployment.active_version_id)
```

For production, picking the immediately-previous version is usually correct. For incidents, you may need to go further back if multiple recent versions share the bug.

## Rolling forward after rollback

After a rollback, the version you rolled back FROM is still in `ready` state (unless you explicitly archive it). You can re-promote it later if it turns out the issue wasn't in the code:
```typescript
await miosa.deployments.versions.promote(deploymentId, originalVersionId)
```

This is a regular promotion, not a rollback. The path is symmetric.

## What rollback doesn't fix

| Issue | Why rollback doesn't help |
|---|---|
| Bad database migration | The database is *outside* the version. Roll back the schema separately or restore from backup. See [Postgres](/docs/data/postgres). |
| Bad managed-data state | Same: data services persist across version changes by design. |
| External service config drift | Stripe webhooks, OAuth callbacks, and similar: not part of the release. |
| Already-served bad responses | Already in your customers' browsers / caches. Bust caches separately. |

Rollback fixes code; it does not fix state. Plan migrations to be backward-compatible (`expand → migrate → contract`) so older versions keep working after a forward migration.

## Idempotency

Rollback requests carry an `Idempotency-Key` header. Identical keys within the retention window return the original result without re-running the operation. This matters during incidents when retry storms are common.

## Audit

Every rollback emits an audit event with:

- The previous `active_version_id`
- The target version_id
- The user / API key that performed it
- The `Idempotency-Key`
- External attribution

Audit events are queryable through the platform audit API and are retained per the tenant's plan.

docker-host/runtime-instances:
A **Runtime Instance** is a running production runtime that serves a dynamic deployment. Static deployments do not have runtime instances; they are served from immutable static artifacts.

> **Note: Phase status**
>
> The caller-facing contract is stable: dynamic deployments start production runtimes, wait for health checks, and only promote when the new version is ready. You do not need to know how MIOSA places or reconciles those runtimes.

## What a runtime instance is

A runtime started from the customer's release. The release is the customer's app, fully packaged. The runtime:

1. Boots in under a few seconds.
2. Receives `PORT` (the release port, unless you set your own), `DATABASE_URL`, `AUTH_URL`, and other env vars injected by MIOSA at boot.
3. Starts the configured `run_command`.
4. Listens on `port`.
5. Responds to `GET health_check_path` with 2xx.
6. Joins the deployment's backend pool; the router starts sending it traffic.

When a runtime instance dies (crash, host failure, configured restart), MIOSA's reconciler notices and schedules a replacement on another healthy host.

## Where it runs

Each runtime instance runs in its own microVM on a MIOSA-managed host.
Runtimes of different customers are segmented from each other on the network, and a runtime can reach only the services you have linked to it plus the public internet.
A restart of the host's agent does not stop a running instance.
The agent reattaches to it when it comes back.

## The port your app must use

MIOSA sets `PORT` to the release's port (the service `port`, `8080` by default) unless you set `PORT` yourself in the deployment's env vars.
Your app must listen on that port on all interfaces (`0.0.0.0`), not only on `127.0.0.1`.
MIOSA reaches it from inside the microVM and publishes it at the instance's address.
The address and port the API reports for an instance are where MIOSA's router reaches it, and are not always the runtime's private address.

## Next.js apps

Set `output: "standalone"` in `next.config`.
When the build produces `.next/standalone/server.js`, MIOSA copies `public` and `.next/static` beside it and runs:

```bash
HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0 node .next/standalone/server.js
```

A standalone release carries its own traced `node_modules`, so MIOSA does not reinstall dependencies in the runtime.
Without standalone output, a Next.js app starts with `next start` and needs the full build.

## Build output is required

A Next.js release must contain its production build: `.next/BUILD_ID` has to exist in the release.
A release that is only the source tree cannot run, because `next start` stops at once with `Could not find a production build`.
MIOSA refuses such a release at publish time and again at start time, with the error `build_output_missing`.
Fix it by running the build before the release is created, or by letting MIOSA build the app, and publish again.

## When a start fails

A runtime instance start fails, and the instance is removed, when any of these happens:

| Error | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `release_install_failed` | Downloading, verifying or unpacking the release failed. The error carries the exit code and the last output of the step. |
| `build_output_missing` | A Next.js release has no production build (see above). |
| `app_launch_failed` | The start command could not be launched. |
| `app_not_listening` | The app started but did not answer its health check on its port. |

For `release_install_failed`, `app_launch_failed` and `app_not_listening`, the deployment's error message includes the tail of the app's log, the processes running in the runtime, and the ports it is listening on, so you can see why it did not come up.
Read it first: the usual causes are an app that binds `127.0.0.1` instead of `0.0.0.0`, a wrong `port`, a missing dependency, or a missing build.
Because the failed instance is removed, a start that fails never serves traffic and the previous version stays live.

## What you control vs what MIOSA controls

| You | MIOSA |
|---|---|
| Release contents (your code + dependencies) | Where to schedule instances |
| `run_command` and `port` | When to start / stop / replace instances |
| `health_check_path` | Routing healthy instances to traffic |
| Desired replica count (eventually; defaults to 1) | Boot-time env var injection |
| Env vars set on the deployment | Telemetry, logs streaming |

You don't pick a host directly. MIOSA's scheduler matches your workload's requirements (CPU, RAM, region) against the fleet's free capacity.

## Lifecycle

pending goes to starting on scheduled; starting goes to healthy on checks pass; healthy goes to stopping on tear down; stopping goes to stopped.

starting goes to unhealthy on checks fail; unhealthy goes to stopping on replaced.

starting goes to failed on crashloop budget spent.

- `pending`: scheduled, not yet booting.
- `starting`: VM is booting; health check not yet passing.
- `healthy`: serving traffic.
- `unhealthy`: failing health checks; router has removed it from the pool. Reconciler decides whether to restart or replace.
- `stopping` / `stopped`: deliberately torn down.
- `failed`: terminal, having exceeded the crashloop budget. Reconciler stops trying.

## Health checks and the grace period

When a runtime instance starts, it has a configurable grace period (default 60s) to become healthy. During grace, repeated 5xx / connection-refused are tolerated.

After grace, the health check is enforced strictly:

- 3 consecutive failures → instance marked `unhealthy`, removed from routing.
- If a replacement is needed and starts healthily, the old instance is torn down.
- Repeated rapid failures invoke crashloop backoff: 1s → 2s → 5s → 30s → 5min between restart attempts.

## Blue/green during publish

When you publish a new dynamic version, MIOSA does NOT terminate the existing healthy instances first. The sequence is:

1. Start new runtime instances from the new release.
2. Wait until enough new instances pass health checks.
3. Update the router so the deployment's hostname points at the new instances.
4. Drain (stop accepting new connections) and tear down old instances after old in-flight requests complete.

If step 2 never succeeds, step 3 never runs. The old version stays live, the new version is marked `failed`.

## Replicas

By default, a dynamic service has 1 replica. Increase by setting `desired_replicas` on the service. The reconciler spreads replicas across hosts and across availability zones where possible.
```typescript
await miosa.services.update(serviceId, { desiredReplicas: 3 })
```

Traffic load-balances across all healthy replicas in round-robin (or hash-based if sticky sessions are configured).

## Resource sizing

| Spec | Default | Tunable per service |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | 1 vCPU | yes |
| Memory | 512 MB | yes |
| Disk | 1 GB ephemeral | yes |
| GPU | none | not available (GPU is not productized) |
| Outbound bandwidth | metered | yes |

Sizing is per-service, per-deployment. A worker service can be smaller than a web service.

## Logs

Runtime instances stream stdout/stderr to MIOSA's log plane. Logs are retained per the tenant's plan (default 7 days). Access them through:

- `GET /api/v1/deployments/:id/logs`: deployment-scoped, all services
- `GET /api/v1/services/:id/logs`: per-service
- `GET /api/v1/runtime-instances/:id/logs`: per-instance

Logs include structured metadata: `service_id`, `runtime_instance_id`, `version_id`, `host_id`. Filter by `external_workspace_id` to scope to a white-label customer.

docker-host/templates:
Docker Host templates are curated app shapes for agents, SDKs, and the UI. They do not replace your project code. They provide Dockerfile, Compose, command, port, environment, persistence, and design-context defaults before a sandbox or repository is published.

| Template                      | Best for                                          | Runtime        |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| Next.js App                   | SaaS portals, dashboards, client apps             | Node           |
| Next.js Funnel / Landing Page | funnels, lead magnets, campaign sites             | Node           |
| Vite React SPA                | static React apps, calculators, widgets           | Nginx          |
| Express / Node API            | webhooks, integrations, lightweight APIs          | Node           |
| FastAPI Service               | Python APIs, AI helper services, data tools       | Python         |
| Static HTML Site              | documents, one-page tools, static downloads       | Nginx          |
| Compose Full-Stack App        | web + API + worker + Postgres + Redis on one host | Docker Compose |

Template metadata is returned by:

```text
GET /api/v1/docker-deploy/templates
GET /api/v1/docker-deploy/templates/:id
```

Use a template id as metadata when creating a deployment so the deployment center can show the intended build shape and recover the defaults later:

```json
{
  "deployment_product": "docker_deploy",
  "metadata": {
    "docker_deploy_template_id": "compose-full-stack"
  }
}
```

- [Docker Hosts](/docs/docker-host/hosts): The workspace host that runs Docker Host containers.
- [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing): The publish pipeline that produces a release artifact.
docker-host/versions:
Each successful publish produces a **Deployment Version**. Versions are immutable: the source hash, artifact hash, build log, and runtime config are frozen at creation. Versions never change after they're written.

How Deployments, Versions, and Releases relate:

```mermaid
graph TB
    DEP[Deployment team-portal] -->|active_version_id| V3[Version v3 - active]
    DEP -->|history| V2[Version v2 - archived]
    DEP -->|history| V1[Version v1 - archived]
    V3 -->|artifact_uri| R3[Release sha256:abc]
    V2 -->|artifact_uri| R2[Release sha256:def]
    V1 -->|artifact_uri| R1[Release sha256:ghi]
```

## Version shape
```json
{
  "id": "ver_01H...",
  "deployment_id": "dep_01H...",
  "tenant_id": "...",
  "created_by": "user_...",
  "external_workspace_id": "acct-123",
  "external_user_id": "user-456",
  "external_project_id": "landing-page-789",
  "source_sandbox_id": "sbx_...",
  "build_id": "bld_...",
  "version_number": 17,
  "kind": "static",
  "state": "ready",
  "artifact_uri": "s3://miosa-releases/dep_.../ver_.../dist.tar.zst",
  "artifact_manifest": { "files": 42, "total_bytes": 184320, "entrypoint": "index.html" },
  "artifact_sha256": "a5e6f0c1...",
  "runtime_image": null,
  "runtime_command": null,
  "runtime_port": null,
  "health_check_path": null,
  "build_log_uri": "s3://miosa-logs/builds/bld_.../log.txt",
  "metadata": { },
  "promoted_at": "2026-05-14T18:20:00Z",
  "archived_at": null,
  "created_at": "2026-05-14T18:19:48Z",
  "updated_at": "2026-05-14T18:20:00Z"
}
```

For dynamic versions, the `runtime_image`, `runtime_command`, `runtime_port`, and `health_check_path` fields are populated; for static they're null.

## States

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `created` | Row exists, build not started |
| `building` | Build in progress |
| `ready` | Build succeeded, artifact uploaded, can be promoted |
| `failed` | Build failed or health checks didn't pass; not promotable |
| `archived` | Promoted-out-of; still bootable for rollback |

`state` transitions are one-way (no `ready → failed` after the fact); once a version is `ready`, it stays bootable until explicitly garbage-collected.

## Endpoints
```http
GET    /api/v1/deployments/:id/versions
GET    /api/v1/deployments/:id/versions/:version_id
POST   /api/v1/deployments/:id/versions/:version_id/promote
POST   /api/v1/deployments/:id/rollback
```

### List versions

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const versions = await miosa.deployments.versions.list(deploymentId, {
  limit: 50,
  state: "ready",
})

for (const v of versions.data) {
  console.log(v.version_number, v.kind, v.state, v.artifact_sha256.slice(0, 8))
}
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/versions?state=ready \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

### Promote a specific version

Useful for staged rollouts: publish without auto-promote, manually promote when ready.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const result = await miosa.deployments.versions.promote(deploymentId, versionId)
console.log(result.deployment.active_version_id) // === versionId
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/versions/$VER/promote \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

Requires `deployments:write` scope. Listing/showing requires `deployments:read`.

## Versions and external attribution

Every version inherits attribution from the source sandbox or the publish call. Filtering versions by `external_workspace_id` shows all versions any of your external workspaces published, scoped to your MIOSA tenant.
```typescript
const acmeVersions = await miosa.deployments.versions.list(deploymentId, {
  externalWorkspaceId: "acme-team-123",
})
```

This is how white-label platforms expose a "deploy history" view per end-customer in their own UI.

## How long are versions kept?

`ready` versions are kept for at least 30 days by default. Archived versions older than that are eligible for garbage collection of their release artifacts; the version row itself stays for audit. Long-term storage policies are configurable per tenant. Contact support if you need a different retention.
